passages.text: Comprehensive analysis of mitochondrial and nuclear DNA variations in patients affected by hemoglobinopathies: A pilot study

The hemoglobin disorders are the most common single gene disorders in the world. <sentence_start/>Previous studies have suggested that they are deeply geographically structured and a variety of genetic determinants influences different clinical phenotypes between patients inheriting identical β-globin gene mutations. <sentence_start/>In order to get new insights into the heterogeneity of hemoglobin disorders, we investigated the molecular variations on nuclear genes (i.e. <italic toggle="yes">HBB</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">HBG2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BCL11A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">HBS1L</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">MYB)</italic> and mitochondrial DNA control region. <sentence_start/>This pilot study was carried out on 53 patients belonging to different continents and molecularly classified in 4 subgroup: β-thalassemia (<italic toggle="yes">β</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>+</sup></italic><italic toggle="yes">/β</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>+</sup></italic>, <italic toggle="yes">β</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>0</sup></italic><italic toggle="yes">/β</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>0</sup></italic> <italic toggle="yes">and β</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>+</sup></italic><italic toggle="yes">/β</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>0</sup></italic>)(15), sickle cell disease <italic toggle="yes">(HbS/HbS</italic>)(20), sickle cell/β-thalassemia (<italic toggle="yes">HbS/β</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>+</sup></italic> <italic toggle="yes">or HBS/β</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>0</sup></italic>)(10), and non-thalassemic compound heterozygous (<italic toggle="yes">HbS/HbC</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">HbO-Arab/HbC</italic>)(8). <sentence_start/>This comprehensive phylogenetic analysis provided a clear separation between African and European patients either in nuclear or mitochondrial variations. <sentence_start/>Notably, informing on the phylogeographic structure of affected individuals, this accurate genetic stratification, could help to optimize the diagnostic algorithm for patients with uncertain or unknown origin.
Author summary

Worldwide most frequent genetic diseases are represented by a very heterogeneous group of congenital hemolytic anaemias which include β-thalassemia and sickle cell anaemia. <sentence_start/>They are deeply geographically structured and characterized by high complexity of the genetic background associated with variable clinical severities. <sentence_start/>Due to this heterogeneity we investigated the nuclear and mitochondrial DNA marker variations in patients with hemoglobinopathies in order to provide the first comprehensive genetic stratification of these hereditary disease. <sentence_start/>This study contributes to detail the multifaceted picture of hemoglobin disorders.
Introduction

Worldwide, the most frequent genetic diseases are represented by a very heterogeneous subgroup of congenital hemolytic anaemias, which includes β-thalassemia and sickle cell anaemia [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref001" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1749-6632.2010.05546.x" pmid="20712767" count="1">1</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Individuals with β-thalassemia have a diverse range of clinical manifestations, from an asymptomatic state to a transfusion-dependent form, depending mainly on the β-globin gene mutations [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref002" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bcmd.2008.06.007" pmid="18691915" pmcid="PMC4100606" count="1">2</citation>,<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref003" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60283-3" pmid="21908035" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, individuals with identical β-thalassemia genotypes can exhibit variable clinical severities [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref004" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1182/asheducation-2013.1.354" pmid="24319204" count="1">4</citation>], because of the high complexity of the genetic background associated with the disease [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref005" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkt911" pmid="24137000" pmcid="PMC3964999" count="1">5</citation>,<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref006" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bpobgyn.2016.10.013" pmid="27847257" count="1">6</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The term sickle cell disease (SCD) encompasses a group of disorders characterized by the presence of at least one hemoglobin S allele (HbS; p.Glu6Val in <italic toggle="yes">HBB</italic>) and a second <italic toggle="yes">HBB</italic> allele carrying pathogenic variant resulting in abnormal hemoglobin polymerization. <sentence_start/>SCD (HbS/HbS) caused by the homozygous <italic toggle="yes">HBB</italic> variant p.Glu6Val is the most common cause of SCD in the US. <sentence_start/>SCD caused by compound heterozygous <italic toggle="yes">HBB</italic> pathogenic variants includes sickle-hemoglobin C disease (HbS/HbC) and two types of sickle β-thalassemia (HbS/β<sup>+</sup>-thalassemia and HbS/β°-thalassemia). <sentence_start/>Other β-globin chain variants such as D-Punjab, O-Arab, and E also result in SCD when inherited with HbS. The marked variability in phenotype severity is due to the different genotypes of the disease and the co-presence of other independent genetic factors that may worsen or alleviate the phenotype [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref007" ref-type="bibr" count="1">7</citation>,<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref008" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11033-014-3195-5" pmid="24488321" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Single nucleotide polymorphism (SNPs) in several genetic modulators and <italic toggle="yes">cis</italic>-regulatory elements involved in the regulation of human HbF, i.e. <italic toggle="yes">HBG2</italic>, B cell CLL/lymphoma 11A (<italic toggle="yes">BCL11A</italic>), Kruppel-like factor 1 (<italic toggle="yes">KLF1</italic>) and <italic toggle="yes">MYB</italic>, can delay fetal-to-adult hemoglobin (Hb) switch, ameliorating the severity of β-thalassemia and sickle cell disease [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref009" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bcmd.2017.01.011" pmid="28160732" count="1">9</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref020" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bcmd.2015.01.001" pmid="25703683" pmcid="PMC4341902" count="1">20</citation>].

Other studies focusing on different human populations reported that the SNPs are deeply geographically structured and further loci i.e <italic toggle="yes">KCNK10</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">GPR65</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RNASE2</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">RNASE3</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">C/EBPE</italic> are involved in HbF expression regulation [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref021" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/ajh.22221" pmid="22139998" pmcid="PMC3302931" count="1">21</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref025" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/03630269.2016.1252386" pmid="27829304" count="1">25</citation>].

In the last decades, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) has been proven to be an effective tool to reconstruct the maternal origins of individuals and geographically map samples, but it also plays a key role in various human diseases. <sentence_start/>Due to its maternal inheritance and the lack of recombination [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref026" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/hmg/dds435" pmid="23077218" pmcid="PMC3526165" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref027" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-biochem-060815-014402" pmid="27023847" count="1">27</citation>], its differentiation is generated only by the sequential accumulation of new mutations from a female ancestor that makes the mtDNA a molecular register along maternal lines. <sentence_start/>Over millennia, the molecular differentiation gave rise to groups of mtDNAs that share a set of variants (called haplotypes) acquired from the same common female ancestor. <sentence_start/>Even though whole genomic approaches are now answering to questions related to the origin and diversification of species, the mtDNA continues to be an important source of information to reconstruct the genetic history of specific populations. <sentence_start/>Studies based on sequence variation especially in the noncoding control region have allowed the classification of distinct geographic and ethnic affinities [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref028" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7688932" pmcid="PMC1682412" count="1">28</citation>-<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref034" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00414-004-0466-z" pmid="15248073" count="1">34</citation>].

Nowadays, a detailed worldwide mtDNA phylogeny is available, where different haplogroups are defined by specific mutational motifs and restricted to specific areas and population groups [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref035" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.1135566" pmid="17170302" count="1">35</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The development of phylogeography is closely related to mtDNA analysis, which was described as one of the best tools to study population variability [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref036" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13323-015-0022-2" pmid="25798216" pmcid="PMC4367903" count="1">36</citation>].

The consequences of mitochondrial mutations have been also evaluated in human ageing as well as inherited and acquired diseases [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref037" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1146/annurev-biochem-060408-093701" pmid="20350166" count="1">37</citation>,<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref038" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2015.08.067" pmid="26406369" pmcid="PMC4743751" count="1">38</citation>], however the only study focusing on the association of mtDNA variations with β-thalassemia claimed that mitochondrial mutations may increase disease susceptibility or the development of phenotype-associated disease in affected individuals, although concluded that there was no strong proof for the association of these polymorphisms with β-thalassemia [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref039" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3109/19401736.2014.958730" pmid="25230702" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Doubtless, as mentioned above, there should be a correlation between hemoglobinopathies and geographic origins of patients [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref040" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s40291-018-0370-8" pmid="30478714" count="1">40</citation>,<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref041" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15040423" count="1">41</citation>], that could be deepened also by considering the mtDNA variability.

The aim of this pilot study was to provide a first comprehensive analysis of hemoglobin and uniparental marker variants in 53 patients with hemoglobinopathies coming from different countries, in order to depict the phylogeographic structure of affected individuals.
Results and discussion

The study was carried out on 53 patients (M/F: 38/15) affected by hemoglobinophaties who referred to our laboratory at the University of Perugia/Hospital Santa Maria della Misericordia, in Umbria a region of Central Italy.

Except for the first patient for whom we do not know the origin, 16 patients (30.2%) were European, 28 (52.8%) African, four (7.6%) Asian and four (7.6%) American. <sentence_start/>Complete information about geographical characteristics and genotypes were reported in Table 1, while clinical phenotypes were detailed in S1 Text and S1-S4 Tables.

Homozygotes and compound heterozygotes included: 15 β-thalassemia patients, 20 sickle cell disease (HbS/HbS) patients, ten sickle cell/β-thalassemia (HbS/β<sup>+</sup> or β<sup>0</sup>) patients, eight compound heterozygotes for Hb variants of which seven HbS/HbC and one HbO-Arab/HbC. Ten patients carried α mutations: eight were heterozygous for α <sup>-3.7</sup> and two for ααα <sup>anti 3.7</sup> (Table 1). <sentence_start/>Seventeen different mutations of the <italic toggle="yes">HBB</italic> gene were found: 12 generated β-thalassemic defects, two produced Hb thalassemic variants (i.e. Hb-Lepore and HbE) and three were associated with the production of non-thalassemic Hb variants (HbS, HbC and HbO-Arab) (Table 1).

Overall, β-thalassemia patients carried 17 different gene mutations and 12 different genotypes. <sentence_start/>Seven out of 15 patients (46.6%) were European, two (13.3%) were African, four (26.7%) were Asian and one (6.7%) was American. <sentence_start/>No precise information was available for one patient (6.7%) (Table 1).

Sickle cell/β-thalassemia patients were characterized by four different β genotypes while α mutations (ααα <sup>anti 3.7</sup>) were found in two patients from Albania. <sentence_start/>Seven out of eleven patients were Europeans (63.6%), two (18.2%) Africans and one (9%) American (Table 1).

All sickle cell disease patients carried the same β genotype, while the presence of the -α<sup>3.7</sup>/αα genotype was demonstrated in five patients and the -α<sup>3.7</sup>/-α<sup>3.7</sup> genotype was highlighted in one patient. <sentence_start/>Sixteen out of 20 (80%) were African patients, two were Americans (10%) and two were Europeans (10%) (Table 1).

Moreover, seven out of eight patients included in the cohort of compound heterozygotes who carried HbS/HbC genotype (patients 46-51, 53), while the other patient bore HbC/HbO-Arab genotype (patient 52). <sentence_start/>-α<sup>3.7</sup>/αα genotype was reported in two HbS/HbC cases. <sentence_start/>All eight patients were African (Table 1).
Hemoglobin phenotype modulating SNPs: Geographical distribution

The analysis of the five polymorphic loci related to HbF expression (i.e. <italic toggle="yes">HBG2</italic> rs7482144 [C>T], <italic toggle="yes">BCL11A</italic> rs1427407 [G>T], <italic toggle="yes">BCL11A</italic> rs10189857 [A>G], <italic toggle="yes">HBS1L</italic> rs28384513 [A>C], <italic toggle="yes">HBS1L-MYB</italic> rs9399137 [T>C]), showed <italic toggle="yes">BCL11A rs10189857 [A>G]</italic> as the most frequent polymorphic site, since the allele G was detected in 33/53 patients (21 heterozygotes, 12 homozygotes). <sentence_start/>Conversely, <italic toggle="yes">HBS1L-MYB rs9399137 [T>C]</italic> was the less frequent polymorphic variation, as the allele C was present only in 6/53 patients (one homozygote and five heterozygotes). <sentence_start/>As referring to the other SNPs: <italic toggle="yes">HBG2</italic> rs7482144 [C>T], <italic toggle="yes">BCL11A rs1427407 [G>T]</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">HBS1L-MYB [A>C]</italic> were detected in pts 9, 19 and 21 respectively, showing an intermediate frequency. <sentence_start/>No patients carrying <italic toggle="yes">C/EBPE rs45496295 [C>T]</italic> variation were found (Table 2, S5 Table).

Interestingly, we observed that frequencies of the five analysed SNPs were related to the geographical origin of patients (Fig 1). <sentence_start/>Although in our cohort there were only four Asian cases, all investigated SNPs were detected. <sentence_start/>Conversely, in the other patients (i.e. Europeans, Africans, Americans), the frequency of each SNP was considerably different. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">HBS1L-MYB</italic> rs9399137 T>C was not detected in both our African or American populations, while <italic toggle="yes">HBG2</italic> rs7482144 C>T was not detected in European patients (Fig 1, Table 2, S1A and S1B Fig).
Fig 1
Nuclear SNP frequencies and geographic distribution of five nuclear SNPs in the 53 patients.

Black rings represent the number of patients in different geographic areas. <sentence_start/>Pie charts represent the frequencies of each SNP. <sentence_start/>The central number indicates the total alleles carrying SNPs.

In particular, <italic toggle="yes">HBG2</italic> rs7482144 [C>T] was found in nine patients, five African, three Americans and one Asian (S1A Fig, Table 2). <sentence_start/>The absence of this variation in European subjects did not completely fit with the allele frequencies retrieved from GnomAD database, which reported T alleles in the European population, although in a lower frequency (3839 T alleles and 10893 C alleles) (S1B and S1C Fig).

<italic toggle="yes">BCL11A</italic> rs1427407 [G>T] spread over all analysed ethnic group: 13 African patients, four Europeans, one American and one Asian. <sentence_start/>Likewise, <italic toggle="yes">BCL11A</italic>, rs10189857 [A>G] was present in 33/53 patients: 14 Africans, ten Europeans, four Asians, four Americans and no precise ethnic information were available for one patient (S1A Fig, Table 2). <sentence_start/>The allele frequencies of both <italic toggle="yes">BCL11A</italic> rs1427407 and <italic toggle="yes">BCL11A</italic> rs10189857 were in agreement with those reported in GnomAD database (Fig 1B and 1C).

<italic toggle="yes">HBS1L-MYB</italic> rs28384513 [A>C] was identified in ten African patients, nine Europeans and two Asians, while it was not detected in American patients (Fig 1A, Table 2). <sentence_start/>Notably GnomAD database reported the G allele also in this population, although in a lower frequency (9164 T alleles and 5824 G alleles) (S1B and S1C Fig). <sentence_start/>The low number of American patients included in our cohort (i.e. three pts) could explain the discrepancy between our results and the database.

Finally, the <italic toggle="yes">HBS1L-MYB</italic> rs9399137 [T>C], was detected only in 6/53 analysed patients, five European patients and one Asian (S1A and S1B Fig, Table 2). <sentence_start/>No African patients with <italic toggle="yes">HBS1L-MYB</italic> rs9399137 [T>C] were found in our cohort although this represented the largest group. <sentence_start/>Allele frequencies obtained by GnomAD database reported C alleles in American and African populations, although at lower frequencies (S1B and S1C Fig).

In conclusion, for three out of five SNPs our results were in agreement with GnomAD database. <sentence_start/>The only discrepancy regards <italic toggle="yes">HBG2 rs7482144 [C>T]</italic> which was not detected in European patients and <italic toggle="yes">HBS1L-MYB</italic> rs9399137 [T>C] which was not detected in Africans although these patients represented 30.2% and 52.8% of the cohort, respectively. <sentence_start/>These discrepancies may be due to a selection bias as European patients represented only Italian and Albania geographical areas, while 24/28 African patients came from seven Sub-Saharan countries and only 4/28 came from two North Africa countries. <sentence_start/>(Fig 1)
Analysis of mtDNA sequence variation and integration with hemoglobin marker variants

Mitochondrial control region sequences ranged from nucleotide position (np) 16024 to np 210, thus encompassing the HVSI and most of the HVSII (Table 2). <sentence_start/>The overall sequence alignment of samples revealed 99 polymorphic sites (S), represented by ten transversions and two indel (one deletion and one insertion). <sentence_start/>Nucleotide diversity (π) across all samples was estimated at 0.0173. <sentence_start/>The haplotype diversity was very high (Hd = 0.993) as well as the average number of nucleotide differences (k = 13,052).

When aligned to the revised Cambridge Reference Sequence, a total of 44 different haplotypes were obtained and classified through their mutational motifs into 13 different macro-haplogroups: B, D, G, JT, L0, L1, L2, L3*, M*, N9, R0, UK and X (Fig 2A). <sentence_start/>Seven haplotypes were shared between two or three samples, but five couples of those individuals declared to be maternally related. <sentence_start/>For the remaining two haplotypes, one (HT02) was found in two brothers from Algeria and one sample from Morocco the other (HT04) was detected in one patient from Ivory Coast and one from Benin.
Fig 2
Haplogroup frequency.

(A) Haplogroup frequency pie chart. <sentence_start/>(B) Geographic distribution of patients based on their declared origin and reported for different haplogroups. <sentence_start/>(C) Distribution of hemoglobinopathies subgroups in all patients for different mtDNA haplogroups.

In order to better define the phylogenetic relationships between samples, we have constructed the network illustrated in Fig 3. <sentence_start/>Haplogroup labels are reported according to the Phylotree nomenclature [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref042" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.20921" pmid="18853457" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The network topology showed two major mtDNA clusters, corresponding to super-haplogroups R and not-R. Within R, JT and H haplogroups prevailed. <sentence_start/>The latter formed a star-like cluster mainly represented by sub-haplogroups H1, H2 and H7. <sentence_start/>R0a, HV, B and UK were also represented. <sentence_start/>The not-R cluster included mostly L1, L2 and L3* sub-lineages, followed by L0 and D; also N9, M, X and G were revealed.
Fig 3
Network of mitochondrial variation.

Tree of the 53 mtDNA haplotypes observed among the patients, highlighted with different colors according to their geographic origin. <sentence_start/>The circles are proportional to the number of samples carrying the same haplotype. <sentence_start/>Haplogroups and sub-haplogroups are indicated with capital letters. <sentence_start/>Super-haplogroups R and not-R are defined in the right and left box, respectively.

Among samples, the most represented lineage belonged to the super-haplogroup L (45%), consisting in L0 (8%), L1 (17%), L2 (54%) and L3* (21%), followed by R0 (25%) and M* (13%) (Fig 2B). <sentence_start/>The sibling haplogroup JT was detected with 9% of frequency, while B, N9, UK and X lineages were represented by only one sample each.

It is known that macro-haplogroup L represents the most ancestral mitochondrial lineage of all living modern humans and, if excluding the derived L3 branches M and N, it represents the majority of the typical sub-Saharan mtDNA variability. <sentence_start/>Within L, L2 is the most common haplogroup in Africa and it has been previously observed throughout the continent [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref043" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.134452.111" pmid="22454235" pmcid="PMC3337428" count="1">43</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Our findings agree with the haplogroup frequency and origin of our samples specifically from Nigeria and Ivory Coast (but also Congo and Benin), except for Syria, from which two samples (brothers) derived. <sentence_start/>L3* was found in two samples from Nigeria, one from Guinea, one from Ghana and one from Italy. <sentence_start/>Even if L haplotypes account for <1% of mtDNAs in Europe, with L1b being the most common haplogroup, frequencies widely change, ranging from 3% in Southern Europe to 0.7% in Central Europe and 0.5% in Northern Europe.

Within R0, only one sample R0a and one HV1 were found, while the remaining patients were H, thus corresponding to a total of 11/53 (21%). <sentence_start/>Haplogroup H is the most frequent mitochondrial lineage in Europe (~40%) with a declining pattern from Western Europe towards the Near East and Caucasus (~10-20%). <sentence_start/>It was also found in Africa, especially the North region, with a peak of H1 in Maghreb and this is in accordance with the origin of our H samples (Italy, Albania, Morocco and Algeria).

As for the macro-haplogroup M, samples originated from Venezuela and Cambodia and belonged to the D4 sub-branches (D1f1 and D4b2d), which exactly reflect the geographic maximum distribution of these lineages (South America and East Asia, respectively) [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref044" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0032179" pmid="22363811" pmcid="PMC3283723" count="1">44</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Even patient 53 from Morocco, belonging to M1a2a mitochondrial haplogroup, was congruent with the frequency distribution of the lineage, unlike African patients 28 and 29 (brothers) and 40, which belonged to G1a and M30c respectively, both sub-lineages typical of Asia.

The East Asian B4 haplogroup revealed in patient 27 from Dominican Republic could result odd, but we should keep in mind that a subclade of B4b is one of the five haplogroups found among indigenous people of the Americas, thus explaining a lower distribution also in Central America.

Patient 13 from China belonging to N9a10a perfectly reflects the East Asian origin and the distribution peak of the lineage [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref045" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2012.03.002" pmid="22482806" pmcid="PMC3322232" count="1">45</citation>].

After evaluating relationships between mitochondrial phylogeny and the geographic origin of individuals, we moved to a different level of resolution, including also the nuclear SNP data in a new network (S2 Fig, Table 2). <sentence_start/>We considered the mitochondrial control-region haplotypes, whose phylogenetic relationships are illustrated in the Fig 3, together with zygosity of the five variable genes, trying to detail the patients’ genotype. <sentence_start/>Patients 5, 14, 29 and 45 were the only homozygous wildtype for all variables: two from Italy (both belonging to the R0 haplogroup) and two from Nigeria (carrying L0 and G mitogenomes). <sentence_start/>A total of 41/53 patients showed the prevalence of wildtype homozygosity, while only six individuals (patients 6, 10, 21, 25, 34 and 44) were heterozygous for three polymorphisms. <sentence_start/>Fourteen patients were homozygous mutants for one SNP, while only patient 15 was homozygous mutant for three variables. <sentence_start/>It is to be highlighted that all individuals within L mitochondrial macro-haplogroup were homozygous wildtype for <italic toggle="yes">HBS1L-MYB</italic> rs9399137 [T>C], as patients harbouring the JT mitochondrial lineage were homozygous wildtype for <italic toggle="yes">HBG2</italic> rs7482144 [C>T]. <sentence_start/>Conversely, <italic toggle="yes">C/EBPE</italic> rs45496295 [C>T] was always found as homozygous wildtype, thus it was excluded from the representation.

A further analysis was performed, trying to obtain a graphical overview of the possible integration between mtDNA control region variability and nuclear mutations associated to hemoglobinopathies subgroups (Table 2, S2 Text and S5 Table). <sentence_start/>In S3 Fig, different phenotypical subgroups were highlighted in the mitochondrial phylogenetic tree: β-thalassemia (β-thal) patients, sickle cell/β-thalassemia (HbS/β<sup>+</sup> or β<sup>0</sup>), sickle cell disease (HbS/HbS) and compound heterozygotes (HbS/HbC and HbO-Arab/HbC). <sentence_start/>The overall network revealed a predominant distribution of the hemoglobinopathies subgroups within clades (S3 Fig). <sentence_start/>In particular, except for three haplotypes belonging to samples from Albania (patient 26) and South America (patiens 27 and 41) that lied in the R clade, sickle cell disease seemed to be common among not-R haplogroups, especially African lineages (L0, L1, L2 and L3*). <sentence_start/>It is to be noticed that no sickle cell disease patients belonged to macro-haplogroup R0 (inclusive of R0a, H and HV haplogroups) (Fig 2C). <sentence_start/>A similar distribution was observed for compound heterozygotes patients, all Africans; they lied in not-R clade (M1, L2 and L3* haplogroups), except for patient 52, from Morocco, that belonged to H1 lineage and it was the only patient characterized by HbC/HbO-Arab genotype. <sentence_start/>An opposite distribution could be observed for thalassemic patients, which spread among R haplogroups, except for four samples from South America (patient 7), Syria (patients 11 and 12, brothers) and Cambodia (patient 15). <sentence_start/>In particular, the R0 clade seemed to be overall characterized by β-thalassemic individuals. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, sickle cell/β-thalassemia patients (HbS/β<sup>+</sup> or β<sup>0</sup>) seemed to be widespread in the network.

When we separated data in four different networks, one for each hemoglobinopathies subgroup coloured with the geographic origin of the patient, it was clear that Asian samples were all thalassemic, but clustered far from European thalassemic patients (S3E Fig). <sentence_start/>No African patient was affected by thalassemia (with the exception of a couple of brothers from Algeria). <sentence_start/>If excluding two samples with sickle cell/β-thalassemia patients (HbS/β<sup>+</sup> or β<sup>0</sup>) (S3F Fig) Africans prevail in sickle cell disease grouping (S3G Fig) and are the only source of compound heterozygotes (S3H Fig). <sentence_start/>No star-like pattern of molecular relatedness emerged that would represent any event of local expansion.

To resume, we observed that European patients fall prevalently into the thalassemic (β<sup>+</sup>/β<sup>+</sup>, β<sup>0</sup>/β<sup>0</sup> and β<sup>+</sup>/β<sup>0</sup>) or sickle cell/β-thalassemia (HbS/β<sup>+</sup> or β<sup>0</sup>) subgroups, while Africans into the remaining two (i.e. HbS/HbS and HbS/HbC) (S4 Fig).

The clear structuring and sub-division between African and European clades could be detected also in the principal component analysis (PCA) performed by considering all variable sites (both nuclear and mtDNA SNPs) for the 53 patients (Fig 4). <sentence_start/>Moreover, American samples lied in two quarters, close to Europeans. <sentence_start/>The graph showed also three European samples close to the African quarters (left quarters): Albanian patients 17 (X haplogroup) and 26 (JT), and patient 35 (L3*) from Italy.
Fig 4

Two-dimensional Principal Component Analysis plot obtained by including all mitochondrial and nuclear DNA variations, considered separately in each sample and coloured depending on their geographic origin.

On the other hand, five African samples stand close to the vertical line that separates left and right quarters: patient 24 (L3*) from Guinea; patients 29 (G), 43 (L3*), and 45 (L0) from Nigeria; and patient 44 (L0) from Congo. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, all these patients together with three Europeans (patients 17, 26, 35) carried at least HbS allele, which is very frequent in the Sub Saharan Africa. <sentence_start/>The prevalently European quarter (the first quarter on the right) shows four African patients (patients 3 and 4 siblings, and patients 48 and 52). <sentence_start/>The two most distant patients from African samples are from North Africa (Morocco and Algeria) confirming the closeness to European ones. <sentence_start/>Intriguingly, only two thalassemic samples lie on the left half of the PCA: they are patients 11 and 12, the only samples from West Asia, while the other two Asian samples were from China and Cambodia, and fall into the right half of the graph.
Even if the past and recent migrations could partially alter the picture, a high level of population and geographic structuring still persist.
Conclusions

This study represents the first comprehensive analysis of nuclear and mitochondrial DNA marker variations in patients with hemoglobinopathies and showed a clear separation between African and European patients allowing for depicting the phylogeographic structure of affected individuals. <sentence_start/>Further investigations on a larger cohort of patients, as well as on additional mitochondrial and nuclear variants using standard and Next Generation Sequencing methodologies, will allow to establish possible correlations between genetic data and clinical behaviour. <sentence_start/>Taking all together, this pilot study based on hemoglobin and uniparental marker variants could represent an integrated and powerful tool for enliven the multifaced pictures of hemoglobinophaties.
Materials and methods
Patients and DNA extraction

The study was carried out on 53 patients (M/F: 38/15) affected by hemoglobinophaties who referred to our laboratory at the University of Perugia/Hospital Santa Maria della Misericordia, in Umbria a region of Central Italy. <sentence_start/>(Table 1). <sentence_start/>α and β genotype of patients 1-12, 16-23, 26-39 and 46-52 were previously described [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref046" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/03630269.2017.1289101" pmid="28361595" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Moreover patients 3-4, 11-12, 16-17 and 47, 49-50 were brothers. <sentence_start/>Patient 21 was mother of patient 7.

Peripheral blood samples were collected during routine medical examinations and genomic DNA was isolated through salting-out procedure [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref047" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/16.3.1215" pmid="3344216" pmcid="PMC334765" count="1">47</citation>].

At diagnosis and/or during follow-up all patients or their parents/guardians provided informed consent for sample collection, storage and for research collaborative studies. <sentence_start/>Protocols were approved by the Ethics Committee for Clinical Experimentation of the University of Perugia (protocol no. 2017-01) and analyses were performed in agreement with the Helsinki declaration.
Genomic DNA analysis

Five SNP associated with phenotype severity modulating respectively <italic toggle="yes">HBG2</italic> rs7482144 [C>T], <italic toggle="yes">BCL11A</italic> rs1427407 [G>T], <italic toggle="yes">BCL11A</italic> rs10189857 [A>G], <italic toggle="yes">HBS1L</italic> rs28384513 [A>C] and <italic toggle="yes">HBS1L-MYB</italic> rs9399137 [T>C] were studied in all patients, using polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based reverse dot-blot technique (β-Thal Modifier StripAssay; ViennaLab Diagnostics GmbH, Vienna, Austria).

<italic toggle="yes">C/EBPE</italic>, rs45496295 [C>T] were studied using primers: <italic toggle="yes">CEBP_F</italic>: <monospace>5’-GACAGGAGCTGGCTCTGAGT-3’</monospace> and <italic toggle="yes">CEBP_R</italic>: <monospace>5’-TCCGCAGAGTTAGGCCGT-3’</monospace>

Nucleotide Sequencing was performed using BigDye<sup>TM</sup> Terminator Cycler Sequencing Kit and ABI PRISM<sup>TM</sup> 310 Genetic Analyzer (PE Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref048" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.74.12.5463" pmid="271968" pmcid="PMC431765" count="1">48</citation>].
The SNP frequency in the different populations were obtained by GnomAD database (Genome Aggregation Database, ).
Mitochondrial DNA analysis

Mitochondrial control region between sites 15877 and 259 was amplified using two primers designed on the revised Cambridge Reference Sequence (rCRS) with accession number [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref049" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/13779" pmid="10508508" count="1">49</citation>]: forward <monospace>5’-CAAATGGGCCTGTCCTTGTA-3’</monospace> and reverse <monospace>5’-TGTGCAGACATTCAATTGTT-3’</monospace>. <sentence_start/>The PCR fragments were first enzymatically purified (ExoSAP-IT®, USB Corporation, Cleveland, OH, USA), then cycle sequenced by application of ABI Prism™ BigDye Terminator chemistry on the ABI PRISM<sup>TM</sup> 310 Genetic Analyzer (PE Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA), with the forward primer <monospace>5’-CCATTAGCACCCAAAGCTA-3’</monospace>.

Sequences were assembled and aligned to rCRS using Sequencher™ 5.10 (Gene Codes Corporation). <sentence_start/>Whenever electropherograms showed ambiguities, new PCR amplifications and sequencing reactions were performed.

Final assembling encompassed at least the entire Hyper Variable Sequence HVSI and part of HVSII (from np 16024 to np 210). <sentence_start/>All mitochondrial control-region sequences were deposited in GenBank with accession numbers .

For each sample, haplotypes were registered and classified in haplogroups according to the respective mutational motifs by referring to HaploGrep2 software based on PhyloTree database build 17, [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref042" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.20921" pmid="18853457" count="1">42</citation>].
Genetic variation indices were estimated by using DnaSP 5.1 software [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref050" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btp187" pmid="19346325" count="1">50</citation>].
The evolutionary relationships among haplotypes were visualized through the construction of a median-joining network using Network 10 software ( ).

By default, all polymorphisms relative to rCRS were weighted by a value of ten, except for the highly variable site 16519 and the variations in the poly-C stretch around np 16189 that were down-weighted to one. <sentence_start/>Conversely, triple weights were assigned to the mutational motifs 16223 and 73 in order to strengthen the topology of the network.

Principal component analyses (PCA) were performed using Excel software implemented by XLSTAT, as described elsewhere [<citation rid="pone.0240632.ref051" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0153004" pmid="27054850" pmcid="PMC4824442" count="1">51</citation>] in order to explain the variance of multivariate data (mitochondrial and nuclear DNA variation, considered separately in each sample).
